name: 1st Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 5th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 6th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 7th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: Georgia Street
after: Likely {{the state}}

name: Georgia Street
after: Georgia Herrick Bell (1845–1899), wife of {{Major Horace Bell}}, on whose land the street was laid out

name: Alameda Street
after: Spanish for a tree-lined avenue, from {{álamo}} (“cottonwood tree”)

name: Huber Street
after: Not documented; most likely {{Caroline Howard (née Huber)}}, wife of the tract developer Dr. Frederick Preston Howard — the same inference that explains Carolina Street, one block east, now Hewitt Street.

name: Aztec Avenue
after: The {{Aztec}} empire — one of a conquest theme Andrew Glassell ran through his 1884 subdivision, alongside Cortez Street for Hernán Cortés and Montezuma Avenue (now Dawson Street) for Moctezuma II

name: Patton Street
after: {{George Smith Patton (1856–1927)}}, the attorney who developed the street — nephew and law partner of Andrew Glassell, who subdivided the adjoining tract the following year, and father of the WWII general

name: Garey Street
after: Almost certainly {{Thomas Andrew Garey (1830–1909)}}, citrus nurseryman and co-founder of Pomona — his was the only Garey family in town when the street was named

name: Figueroa Street
after: {{José Figueroa (1792–1835)}}, governor of Alta California 1833–1835

name: Pearl Street
after: No namesake documented in the 1874 council report; in 1897 ex-Mayor J. R. Toberman claimed the naming as his own

name: Grasshopper Street
after: {{The insect}}: grasshoppers crossing this line from the western plains doomed the grape harvest

name: Central Avenue
after: Central not to Los Angeles but to {{Vernon}}, just south of the city limits when it was platted

name: Wolfskill Avenue
after: {{William Wolfskill}}'s old citrus ranch, which the street ran through

name: Towne Avenue
after: {{Alban Nelson Towne}} (1829–1895), general manager of the Southern Pacific Railroad

name: Stanford Avenue
after: {{Leland Stanford}} (1824–1893), president of the Southern Pacific Railroad and governor of California 1862–1863

name: Crocker Street
after: {{Charles Crocker}} (1822–1888), Southern Pacific executive and one of the “Big Four” financiers of the Central Pacific

name: Ruth Avenue
after: Probably {{Ruth R. Wolfskill}} (1881–1968), daughter of Joseph William Wolfskill, on whose orchard the street was laid out — she was five when it was surveyed

name: Ceres Avenue
after: {{Ceres}}, the Roman goddess of agriculture and the harvest

name: San Pedro Street
after: The port town of {{San Pedro}}, which the street ran toward

name: Witmer Street
after: {{Henry Clayton Witmer}} (1856–1909), banker and real-estate developer, whose family's land was Crown Hill

name: Lucas Avenue
after: {{John Henry “J.H.” Lucas}} (1836–1924), attorney, who was selling the tract it was named on

name: Crown Hill Avenue
after: Not documented, but plainly {{Crown Hill}} itself — the rise the street climbs, and the Witmer family's 650 acres

name: 8th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 9th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: Main Street
after: Its standing as the pueblo’s principal street

name: Hill Street
after: {{Bunker Hill}} — the knoll the street runs along, though the hill was not formally named until 1873, later than the street

name: Fort Street
after: {{Fort Moore}}, built on the hill above it after the Mexican–American War

name: Eternity Street
after: The concept of the eternity after death — it led to Calvary Cemetery, established in 1844. Though an 1895 account claims instead that it was so named because it had neither beginning nor end.

name: Hornet Street
after: {{The insect}} — insects were a common naming source in the young pueblo, as with the Calle de los Chapules that became Figueroa

name: Charity Street
after: The virtue

name: Spring Street
after: Possibly {{Trinidad Ortega}} (1832–1903), who was nicknamed “Primavera”

name: College Street
after: Descriptive — a colegio was to be built here

name: Flower Street
after: Supposedly the blossom-covered hills behind it

name: Olive Street
after: {{The olive}} — though no particular tree or grove here is documented

name: Hope Street
after: The virtue — or possibly sheriff and state senator {{Dr. Alexander W. Hope}} (c. 1820–1856), which the sources do not settle

name: Cameron Lane
after: {{Cameron Erskine Thom}} (1825–1915), who owned and subdivided the tract — district attorney, state senator, Confederate captain, and mayor of Los Angeles 1882–1884

name: Alexander Lane
after: {{Alexander Thom}} (c. 1698–1784), Cameron Thom's paternal grandfather, a Clan Cameron Highlander who fled to the American colonies in 1746

name: Catesby Lane
after: The Thom family name — Cameron Thom's son was Charles Catesby Thom, and a brother carried it too

name: Palm Street
after: {{The palm}}, one of four tree and plant names platted together on the Goodwin Tract in Oct. 1886 — Palm, Spruce, Tulip and Willow

name: Spruce Street
after: {{The spruce}}, one of four tree and plant names platted together on the Goodwin Tract in Oct. 1886 — Palm, Spruce, Tulip and Willow

name: Tulip Street
after: {{The tulip}}, one of four tree and plant names platted together on the Goodwin Tract in Oct. 1886 — Palm, Spruce, Tulip and Willow

name: Willow Street
after: {{The willow}}, one of four tree and plant names platted together on the Goodwin Tract in Oct. 1886 — Palm, Spruce, Tulip and Willow

name: Mesquit Street
after: Presumably the mesquite, alongside the Goodwin Tract's other plant names, but nothing documents it.

name: Santee Street
after: {{Milton Santee}} (1835–1901), city councilman 1884–1886, later a mining and railroad investor

name: Los Angeles Street
after: The city itself — ultimately Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles de Porciúncula, the 1769 Spanish naming of {{the river}}

name: Pico Street
after: {{Pío de Jesús Pico}} (1801–1894), the last Mexican governor of Alta California and a major landowner

name: 10th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 11th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 12th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 15th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: 16th Street
after: Its ordinal position in the downtown grid — the numbering system was in place by 1849

name: Castelar Street
after: {{Emilio Castelar}} (1832–1899), president of the First Spanish Republic in 1873–74

name: Temple Street
after: {{Jonathan Temple}} (1796–1866), the Massachusetts trader who reached the pueblo about 1828, opened its first general store and took Mexican citizenship as Juan Temple

name: William Street
after: Probably {{Ozro William Childs}} (1824–1890) himself — the W of “O. W. Childs” is William — or his eldest surviving son, Ozro William Childs Jr. (1865–1933), who was twenty when the tract was recorded

name: Botiller Street
after: The Botiller family, whose ground it crossed: the sheet subdivides the estate of Juana María Reyes de Botiller, distributed to Tadeo Felipe Botiller and Vicenta B. de Ybarrondo by a decree entered Feb. 27, 1888

name: Clark Avenue
after: Wesley Clark, senior partner in the Los Angeles real-estate firm of Clark & Bryan, who owned this tract with Elden P. Bryan

name: Morgan Lane
after: George W. Morgan, one of the three men the tract was subdivided for and, with A. H. Judson, one of the two at whose request it was recorded

name: Scott Avenue
after: Parmer Milton “P. M.” Scott (1822–1900) and Elizabeth Morton Scott (1840–1913), real-estate investors who lived on the street

name: Whisler Street
after: Mrs. Lourena Whisler, the owner at whose request the subdivision was made and recorded

name: Santa Fe Avenue
after: The {{Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway}}, whose passenger depot opened by the street's junction with 1st Street in May 1887

name: Requena Street
after: Almost certainly {{Manuel Requena}} (c. 1802–1876), Campeche-born merchant who settled in Los Angeles in 1834, alcalde under Mexican rule 1844–45, county supervisor, long-serving councilman and briefly acting mayor in 1856, whose own property the street ran through

name: Commercial Street
after: The businesses it was laid out for

name: Beaudry Street
after: {{Prudent Beaudry}} (c. 1819–1893), Montreal-born merchant turned hillside subdivider who developed Bunker Hill, sat on the City Council from 1871 and was mayor from 1874

name: Francisco Street
after: The {{Francisco family}} — an Ohio clan led by Andrew Wiggins “Andy” Francisco (1825–1898), who came to Los Angeles in 1883 and worked in newspapers, real estate and politics — who lived at the corner of 9th and Figueroa

name: Wilshire Boulevard
after: {{H. Gaylord Wilshire}} (1861–1927), developer, publisher and socialist candidate, who subdivided the tract the first stretch ran through

name: Winston Street
after: {{James Brown Winston}} (1820–1884), the city's first health officer, Common Council member, county supervisor and who with his wife operated the Bella Union Hotel, and who had lived on the street

name: Vignes Street
after: The {{Vignes family}}, principally Jean-Louis Vignes (1780–1862), the Bordeaux-born cooper who bought 104 acres beside the El Aliso sycamore and founded California's first commercial winery

name: Kohler Street
after: {{Charles Kohler}} (1830–1887), German-born musician turned wine merchant who with John Frohling built California's largest wine house from 1856 and co-founded Anaheim in 1857, and who worked the Los Angeles vineyards this street crosses

name: Agatha Street
after: Probably {{Agatha Sabichi}} (1871–1963), fourth of the thirteen children of the attorney and council president Frank Sabichi and Magdalena Wolfskill, on whose father's land the street was named

name: Messer Street
after: Almost certainly {{K. Messer}}, the adjoining landowner — the plat that letters this street writes “K. Messer” across the holding along the tract’s northern edge

name: Traction Avenue
after: The {{electric traction motor}} that powered the streetcars running along it

name: Japanese Village Plaza Mall
after: {{Japanese Village Plaza}}, the Little Tokyo shopping centre built around it in 1978

name: Woodworth Court
after: Probably {{Wallace Woodworth}} (1832–1882), an early settler whose adobe and later house stood at Second and San Pedro Streets, on the ground this court occupies
